rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report the authors' own UAV multispectral flights (4 dates, 2017-2019) over three olive groves, visual severity surveys of each tree, polygon cokriging and discriminant analysis (Tables 5-8).
rows.notes: The study only classifies Xfp symptom severity classes from UAV imagery (cross-validated overall accuracy 0.69, early-detection class accuracy 0.77, Tables 7-8). It does not report any result on controlling or limiting the spread of Xylella; the link to control is asserted in the Introduction and Discussion (scouting prioritisation, DSS) but not tested. Detection is a precondition of the claimed control effect, so Q2 is no and upstream is set. Note also that visual rating, not molecular diagnosis, was the ground truth, so even the detection result refers to symptom severity rather than confirmed infection.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 report own UAV multispectral data, tree-by-tree visual surveys and discriminant classification results (Tables 5-8, Figures 8-10).
rows.notes: The study shows that multitemporal UAV multispectral data can classify olive trees into two symptom-severity classes and map a canonical stress indicator (Figure 9) and class predictions with posterior probabilities (Figure 10). It does not report any adoption of targeted prevention or management strategies, nor any outcome of such strategies; the use of the maps to direct scouting and as a decision-support tool is proposed in the Discussion/Conclusions, not demonstrated. Monitoring is a precondition of the claimed management effect, so Q2 is no and upstream is set.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a primary detection/classification study (UAV multispectral + geostatistics + discriminant analysis) of Xylella symptom severity in three Apulian olive groves; it contains no results on disease control, prevention or management outcomes, so both pest_control claims are supported only at the upstream (detection/monitoring) level.
